title: Topologically reconstructing Pancharatnam-Berry phase via encircling exceptional point for chiral spin-orbit interaction steering

paper_content.abstract:
Photonic spin-orbit interaction (SOI) is related to Pancharatnam-Berry (PB) phase, which is
usually imposed on the cross-polarized components of light incident on a metasurface in
broadband manner. However, metasurfaces exhibiting exceptional points (EPs) can block the
cross-polarization conversion channel, hinting at the possibility of EPs influencing SOI. Here, we
demonstrate that the accumulation of PB phase is equivalent to the encircling of an EP, leading to
topologically reconstructed PB phase. Through spin-Hall effect and spin-to-vortex conversion, we
experimentally realize chiral SOI steering within chosen spectral ranges and polarization, showing
suppression, inversion and doubling of the PB phase accumulated via rotation. Our work
introduces the possibility to control SOIs via a topologically reconstructed PB phase, offering
promising possibilities for applications such as information encryption.
paper_content.introduction:
Photonic systems exhibit spin orbit interaction (SOI)1, which describes the coupling between the
spin and orbital angular momentum of light as it propagates through anisotropic media 2,3. This
interaction provides a paradigm for regulating light-matter interaction and has led to various
intriguing phenomena, such as transverse spin 4,5, spin-momentum locking 6,7, and optical force
effects 8. Photonic SOI fundamentally stems from geometric phases: the spin-redirection phase
originating from wavevector evolution in momentum space, and the Pancharatnam-Berry (PB)
phase arising from polarization-state evolution on the Poincaré sphere 9,10. PB phase are widely
used in metasurfaces, a platform composed of periodically arranged sub-wavelength
nanostructures 11-13, to exhibit SOI phenomena, such as the photonic spin Hall effect 14,15, spin-
orbit conversion 16-18, spin-orbit mapping 19, and support applications including optical holography
20-22 and lenses 23. PB phase in metasurfaces are caused by the rotation of nanostructures, and is
imposed on the orthogonal polarization states 24,25. The integration of PB phase with nonlinear
optics 26,27, disorder 28, and phase-change materials (PCMs) 29-31,49 provides a means to steer
photonic spin-orbit interactions and achieve diverse functionalities. Among these methods,
additional tunability is introduced by PCMs, yet with increased fabrication or preservation
demands. Thus, discovering paradigms that use stable materials with simple fabrication to steer
photonic SOI is imperative. Metasurfaces, in addition to being platforms for SOI, are inherently
open systems where each nanostructure continuously exchanges energy with the incident light 32.
Such non-Hermitian systems naturally contain exceptional points (EPs) 32-35. EPs, non-Hermitian
degeneracies where both eigenvalues and eigenvectors degenerate, introduce various phenomena,
including enhanced sensitivity to perturbations, asymmetric mode switching, etc. 36-39. The
significance of EPs varies across different systems, such as micro-ring resonators and acoustic
systems 40-43. In metasurface systems, non-Hermitian Jones matrices serve as effective
Hamiltonians 33-34,44, leading to degenerate eigenstates that correspond to either left-circularly
polarized (LCP) or right-circularly polarized (RCP) states, reflecting the chirality of the EP 34. EPs
in this regime indicate that circular polarization conversion channel can be completely blocked
while leaving the opposite conversion channel unaffected 32. Thus, EPs provide a unique physical
mechanism that governs polarization conversion processes with chirality, and have inspired a
broad range of studies.45-48. As PB phase-mediated SOI processes operate via polarization
conversion, understanding and harnessing the influence of EPs on these processes becomes a
promising task.

Here, we demonstrated EP’s role in PB phase-mediated photonic SOI, and hence revealed three
chiral-sensitive mechanisms that can steer photonic SOI across visible to near-infrared spectra. In
detail, PB phase accumulation via rotation is topologically equivalent to encircling a polarization
conversion singularity, such as an EP, which reveals that PB phase-based SOI processes are
topologically protected. By introducing static elliptical perturbations, a rotational anisotropy is
induced, as their coupling to the main structure changes with rotation. This ensures that the
encircling trajectory avoids full EP collapse, encountering EPs only at discrete points. Such
encounters disrupt topological protection, change the winding number, and trigger three novel
steering mechanisms: chiral SOI suppression, inversion, and doubling (Fig. 1). These correspond
to suppressed, inverted, or doubled PB phase, respectively, at target wavelength range and
polarization. The chirality is governed by the main structure of the meta-atom. To show the
winding number changing mechanisms can steer photonic SOI on the geometric phase level,
photonic spin-Hall effect and spin-to-vortex conversion are both examined across visible and near-
infrared spectra. These effects are experimentally manifested as wavelength-sensitive spin-
dependent splitting in positional space and orbital-angular-momentum (OAM) generation.
Moreover, photonic SOI steering with different chirality and wavelength range is also verified
through experiments. The observed results match well with the simulations and showcase novel
mechanisms to steer SOI via PB phase with different winding numbers, which we term
topologically reconstructed PB phase (TR-PB phase). Different from nonlinear geometric phase
or active metasurfaces, our work fundamentally enriches PB phase accumulation rule with
fabrication simplicity, and adopts stable metal to steer SOI on the fundamental wave via
topological control with controlled chirality. Comparisons are made in Supplementary Table 1.
Our findings open up promising possibilities for the topological control in systems with
singularities 40 and advanced applications such as information encryption 49.

Three phenomena mediated by TR-PB phase are shown in Fig. 1a-c, i. For suppression in Fig. 1a,
wavelength tuning under RCP transforms PB phase from -2θ to a θ independent constant,
decoupling SOI from rotation. This manifests as OAM transition ℓ = -2 to ℓ = 0 in spin-to-vortex
conversion shown in Fig. 1a, ii. The doubling phenomenon results in a PB phase change from −2θ
to −4θ under RCP incidence, as shown in Fig. 1b. For inversion in Fig. 1c, PB phase flips from -
2θ to +2θ by tuning wavelength under RCP incidence, yielding OAM inversion from ℓ = -2 to ℓ =
+2 shown in Fig. 1c, ii. However, LCP incidence maintains +2θ PB phase response throughout all
configurations in Fig. 1a-c, demonstrating the chirality of the phenomena. Meta-atoms, shown in
Fig. 1d-e, integrate rotating dual-L main structures with static perturbation ellipses on a platform
that employs a 160-nm indium-tin-oxide (ITO) film and 40-nm gold layer on glass, without the
use of PCMs. The meta-atoms for Fig. 1Ea, b, ii and Fig. 1c, ii (Marked by black dashed lines) are
schematized in Fig. 1d and Fig. 1e, respectively. These discovered phenomena cannot be
thoroughly interpreted in conventional Poincaré sphere formalism. To resolve this problem, we
adopted a complex plane perspective, reinterpreting PB phase accumulation.

Topological Reconstruction Controlled by a Single EP under Fixed Wavelength
When there is only one EP induced during rotation at a fixed wavelength, chiral SOI suppression
occurs, decoupling the photonic SOI from structural rotation. Here, we designed two metasurfaces
to demonstrate chiral SOI suppression under different chirality and response wavelength using
finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) parameter sweep simulations.

For these simulations, metasurfaces are set to the size of 10 μm * 10 μm, while perfectly matched
layers are applied at the x, y and z directions. We adopted the material parameters from “Au (gold)
Johnson and Christy” for simulating the structures and the refractive index is set to 1.6 for ITO.
Such configuration was applied throughout our work. The chiral SOI suppression was
demonstrated under RCP incidence within the wavelength range of 700-750 nm as shown in Fig.
2a. The meta-atom that we adopted for simulation is shown in Fig. 2a, i. The meta-atom has a
period of 650 nm with the following geometric dimensions: dx = 80 nm, dy = 45 nm, w = 75 nm,
L1 = 263 nm, and L2 = 145 nm. The perturbation ellipse has axes of 75 nm and 37.5 nm. The
centers of the two reference points (red dots) are separated by a displacement of (245 nm, 245 nm).
See supplementary note 2 for specific discussion. The cross-polarization conversion rate and PB
phase response are presented in Fig. 2a, ii-iii, where the x-axis represents rotation angle of the
main structure, and the y-axis represents input wavelength (See the line plots at the wavelengths
where the EPs occur in supplementary note 7, and the opposite chiral incidence results in
supplementary note 8). Only one EP emerge at 43° under 750 nm, with similar EP identified at 2°
under 700 nm incidence, as shown in Fig. 2a, ii. Corresponding PB phase response within the
range in Fig. 2a, iii became nearly rotation independent, which was in stark contrast with PB phase
response outside the EP influenced wavelength. We manifested such chiral SOI suppression in
photonic spin-Hall effect, using metasurface whose meta-atom rotates following equation (5)
shown below. As shown in Fig. 2a, iⅴ-ⅵi, under LCP excitation, output RCP remains leftward
deflected regardless of the excitation wavelength, while under RCP excitation, output LCP remains
rightward deflected until experiencing SOI suppression and becomes non-deflected in the EP
influenced region. Here we take response at 790 nm and 710 nm as an example, as shown in Fig.
2a, iv-ⅵi.

In Fig. 2b, the chiral SOI suppression was demonstrated under LCP incidence within the
wavelength range of 706 - 823 nm, and we manifested it in spin-to-vortex conversion, using
metasurface whose meta-atom rotates following equation (6), with topological charge set to 3 (ℓ =
3). Equations (5-6) are shown below.

L3=185 nm. The perturbation ellipse has axes of 100 nm and 65 nm. The centers of the two

823 nm, with a similar EP identified at 68° under 706 nm incidence. (See the opposite chiral
incidence results in supplementary note 8). It is evident that when wavelength decreases across
823 nm from higher wavelength, PB phase accumulation is suppressed to a trivial case, with nearly
rotation-independent response. As shown in Fig. 2b, iⅴ-ⅵi, the metasurface generates OAM with
ℓ = +3 under LCP excitation above 823 nm (here we take the phase distribution at 850 nm as an
example), and is transformed to a near plane wave phase distribution below 823 nm (here we take
the phase distribution at 800 nm as an example). However, under RCP excitation, ℓ = -3 regardless
of the wavelength shown in Fig. 2b, ⅴi-ⅵi. Fig. 2c, d i-iii details the suppression evolution in the
cross-polarization conversion complex plane and corresponding TR-PB phase response under
wavelengths marked by purple in Fig. 2b, i. In Fig. 2c, ii, the topological protection was disrupted,
and the EP encircling trajectory altered its winding number near 823 nm and stopped encircling
EP (origin) to adopt the trajectory shown in Fig. 2c, iii, which corresponds to a trivial PB phase
response in Fig. 2d, iii. The supplementary movie 1 demonstrates the suppression evolution.
When EPs emerge consecutively while changing wavelength, it exists the possibility of chiral SOI
doubling. As shown in Fig. 2b, ii, multiple EP responses emerged below 730 nm under LCP
incidence, resulting in the doubled PB phase accumulation (+4θ) within the spectral window from
682 to 692 nm, as shown in Fig. 2b, iii. The multiple EP emergence signifies the topological
protection is further disrupted, leading to a winding number of 2, as shown in Fig. 2c, iv, under
wavelength marked by yellow dashed lines in Fig. 2b, ii, for demonstration. The supplementary
movie 8 reveals its evolution. Such a status results in a 4π geometric phase accumulation over 180°
rotation (Fig. 2d, iv) and is verified in experiments shown in Fig. 3e-f, iii. See more discussion of
chiral in supplementary note 9.

It is worth pointing out that EPs despite sharing the same handedness, they may exhibit opposite
phase-increment in the wavelength-angle space, which reflects the opposing topological
manipulations. For instance, in Fig. 2b, ii-iii, the SOI suppression is caused by the black dashed
EP at 823 nm, and is closed by the red dashed EP at 705 nm. The SOI doubling is caused by the
red dashed EP at 691 nm, and is closed by the black dashed EP at 681 nm. Since the winding
number only changes upon traversing an EP, the corresponding low PCR around such transition
has no impact on the TR-PB phase response. See supplementary note 6 for a complete discussion.

Experiments shown in Fig.3 validate chiral SOI suppression via optical setups in Supplementary
Fig. 1 in the supplementary information. The scanning electron micrographs (SEMs) of designed
meta-atoms are displayed in Fig. 3a-b, the scale bars are set to 2 μm, and it is evident that the two
metasurfaces possess main structure with opposite chirality. Spin dependent splitting in Fig. 3c-d,
i-ii, corresponds well to Fig. 2a, iii-ⅵ, demonstrating the consistency with simulations and the
existence of chiral SOI suppression. Similarly, OAM interference pattern in Fig. 3e-f, i-ii, confirms
chiral SOI suppression in spin-to-vortex conversion (with opposite chirality), corresponding to
results simulated in Fig. 2b, iii-ⅵ. Above the wavelength of 820 nm, LCP excitation yields output
with ℓ = +3 and is transitioned to ℓ = 0 under 820 nm. Here we take responses at 850 nm and 800
nm for demonstration, while RCP maintains ℓ = −3 output regardless of wavelength. Experiment
movies are provided in the supplementary movie 2-3 to demonstrate the suppression process for
the spin-dependent splitting and topological charge transitions under RCP or LCP incidence,
respectively, while changing the wavelength. The interference pattern at 730 nm shows that
topological charge has changed from +3 to +6, while the topological charge under RCP excitation
remains ℓ= −3 (Fig. 3 c-d, iii). The corresponding intensity distribution are provided in
Supplementary Fig. 16. The spectral shift of chiral SOI doubling phenomenon from 692 nm
(simulated in Fig. 2d, iv) to 730 nm in experiment arises from the interplay of two factors. First,
disrupting the topological protection of PB phase accumulation with one EP (leading to a winding
number of 0) destabilizes EP encircling evolution on the polarization-conversion complex plane.
It means the actual evolution trajectory in experiment is not the same as the simulation. Second,
fabrication errors and inhomogeneities of meta-atoms also amplify such deviations from simulated
trajectories in Fig. 2c, iv.

Topological Reconstruction Controlled by dual EPs under Fixed Wavelength
The introduction of two exceptional points (EPs) during rotation at a fixed wavelength enables
chiral SOI inversion, reversing the PB phase accumulation principle relative to rotation angle
under target spin. The corresponding numerical simulations and evolution analyses of chiral SOI
inversion are shown in Fig. 4. The meta-atom adopts the configuration in Fig. 4a. It has a period
of 700 nm with the following geometric dimensions: dx =80 nm, dy=45 nm, w=75 nm, L1=263
nm, L2=145 nm. The perturbation ellipses all possess axes of 75 nm and 37.5 nm. The centers of
the four perturbation ellipses and the main structure are separated by an absolute displacement of
(220 nm, 220 nm). The four perturbation ellipses elevate the main structure’s rotational symmetry
from twofold to fourfold, so that two exceptional points can be introduced during a 180° rotation
cycle of the main structure. In Fig. 4b, cross-polarization conversion rate of the meta-atom under
RCP excitation was mapped as a function of the main structure’s rotation angle and input
wavelength. Two EPs are observed at 51° and 141° under the wavelength of 748.12 nm, with
similar EPs identified at 60° and 150° under 691.73 nm incidence. See supplementary note 3 for
EP verification, and also see supplementary note 10 for the near-field analysis of the EP origin.
Correspondingly, the PB phase response in Fig. 4c reveals the opposite PB phase accumulation for
RCP excitation within the spectral window formed by 750nm and 690nm. It is worth pointing out
that the abrupt changes near 700 nm and 742nm in Fig. 4a-b are caused by Rayleigh anomalies,
but it is irrelevant to the inversion process. (See the opposite chiral incidence results in
supplementary note 8). The evolution of EP encirclement and the resulting PB phase accumulation
at wavelengths marked by gray dashed lines are shown in Fig. 4d, ⅰ to ⅳ and Fig. 4e, ⅰ to ⅳ. It can
be clearly seen from Fig. 4d, ⅰ to ⅳ, that the encirclement is clockwise oriented at first, and the
corresponding PB phase declines monotonically with rotation angle -2θ. Further evolving to Fig.
4d, ii, the corresponding PB phase began to decline non-monotonically. In Fig. 4d, iii, two points
simultaneously reach the EP symmetrically, while all other trajectory points remain outside the
singularity.

Such evolution on the complex plane produces the stepwise PB phase distribution observed in Fig.
4e, iii. The progression from Fig. 4d, iii to iv reveals even more intriguing evolution. After
traversing two EPs, the encircling trajectories maintain their original motion, crossing one another,
forming counterclockwise EP encircling path. This evolution manifests as inverted PB phase
accumulation +2θ under RCP incidence that increases monotonically shown in Fig. 3e, iv. The
movie is provided in the supplementary movie 4 to demonstrate such process. Such unconventional
phase behavior arises from the deliberate introduction of EPs during rotation, which disrupts the
topological protection and flips the winding number to +1. Without the EP induced evolution in
the complex plane, neither resonance nor phase-change materials could perturb the conventional
PB phase–rotation correspondence.

TR-PB phase fundamentally enriches metasurface design toolbox. To validate this claim, we
designed three distinct metasurfaces shown in Fig. 4f–h. These metasurfaces demonstrated the
chiral SOI inversion phenomenon either through spin-to-vortex conversion (Fig. 4f-g) or photonic
spin Hall effects (Fig. 4h), satisfying Equation (5) or Equation (6), respectively. For the first
(second) metasurface, the topological charge ℓ is set to 1 (2). The simulation results are shown in
Fig. 4f-g. As wavelength decreases from 800 nm to 710 nm under RCP excitation, topological
charge inverts from ℓ =-1 to +1 in Fig. 4f, i-iv and from ℓ = -2 to +2 in Fig. 4g, i-iv. In contrast,
LCP excitation maintains invariant topological charge across the entire spectrum for both
metasurfaces. For the third metasurface, photonic spin Hall effect is demonstrated under RCP
excitation shown in Fig. 4h, i to iv. The beam deflection shifts from rightward to leftward as the
wavelength decreases from 800 nm to 710 nm. LCP maintains a persistent leftward deflection
without inversion.

Figure 5 experimentally validates chiral SOI inversion via optical setups detailed in Supplementary
Fig. 1 in the supplementary information. Corresponding to simulations in Fig. 4e, topological
charge inversion from ℓ = −1 to ℓ = +1 under RCP excitation as the wavelength shifts from 795
nm to 715 nm are demonstrated in Fig. 5a, while the LCP excitation preserves the topological
charge throughout the spectral range. Similarly, the chiral SOI inversion for ℓ =2 via spin-vortex
conversion is shown in Fig. 5b. Wavelength-driven beam deflection inversion in the spin-Hall
effect is demonstrated in Fig. 5c, i‑iv, matching the simulations in Fig. 4g, i‑iv, with LCP
maintaining persistent leftward deflection. Supplementary movie 5-7 captures experimental
inversion process for both topological charge transitions and spin-dependent splitting under RCP
incidence. While the corresponding intensity distribution are provided in Supplementary Fig. 16.
Control experiments confirm these effects originate solely from TR-PB phase modulation, which
is achieved through anisotropic coupling between main structure and perturbation ellipses, rather
than perturbation ellipse, rotation of the dual-L configuration seen from Supplementary Fig. 9 in
the supplementary materials. The SEM images of the metasurfaces are presented in Fig. 5d. It can
be clearly seen that only the main structures rotate according to Equations (5) and (6), while
perturbation ellipses remain fixed. Scale bars are set to 1 μm.

TR-PB phase used for information encryption
In this work, six possible combinations of meta-atoms are designed, as shown in Fig. 6(a). Their
PB phase responses are catalogued by incident polarization and wavelength in a TR-PB phase
library, shown in Fig. 6 (b), from which the PB phase acquisition rule of any structure under
specific polarization and input wavelength can be directly extracted.

The encryption design workflow is presented in Fig. 6(c). A modified GS algorithm first computes
the near-field phase distributions of the decoy image and the hidden image. The two phase-profiles
are linked through the rules of reversed, doubled, and conventional PB phase accumulation. By
comparing the two distributions, a ternary mask consisting only of values -1, +1, and +2 is obtained.
By consulting the TR-PB library, every specific meta-atom type of the metasurface and the rotation
angle of each main structure are determined , together with the correct decryption key K
4
(σ, λ) that
encodes the required polarization and wavelength. As shown in Fig. 6(d), the hidden image is
retrieved only with the correct key. For instance, under LCP illumination, the PB phase remains
conventional (+2θ) across the entire spectrum, and the reconstructed hologram consistently
displays the cat image (Fig. 6(d), i-ii). In contrast, when the illumination switches to the
polarization corresponding to the REP, the PB phase exhibits inversion and doubling at 730 nm in
our design. As the wavelength changes from 850 nm to 730 nm, the reconstructed hologram
accordingly switches from an inverted cat image (Fig. 6(d), iii) to the dog image (Fig. 6(d), iv). This
spin-decoupling effect, arising from the chiral nature of the proposed TR-PB phase, enables
the observed wavelength and polarization dependent image switching, thereby demonstrating the
information encryption capability.
paper_content.methods:
Device fabrication
The substrate used here is 160 nm ITO-coated silica glass. The substrates were cleaned by
sequential ultrasonication for 5min in acetone, methanol, and ultrapure water. The fabrication
involved electron beam lithography, sequential deposition of a 6nm titanium (Ti) layer and a 40nm
gold (Au) film, and liftoff in butanone.

Optical setup
In order to fully characterize the OAM beams, we used a Mach-Zehnder interferometer as shown
in Supplementary Fig. 1(a). In this configuration, a Ti: Sapphire ultrafast femtosecond laser (pulse
length: ≈115 fs, repetition rate: 76 MHz) centered at 800 nm is used as a light source. A
horizontally-polarized beam is produced by using a linear polarizer (LP1). Then it is split in two
beams by means of a 50/50 beam splitter (BS1). the upper arm of the interferometer passes through
a quarter waveplate (QWP1) to produce a circularly polarized beam. A weakly focusing lens (L1,
f=150 mm) is used to reduce the beam size to be comparable with the diameter of the patterned
metasurface (≈500 μm). A 20× objective lens, a lens (L2, f=150 mm) and a camera behind the
metasurface is used for recording the OAM beam created by the metasurface. The OAM beam
passes through a polarization filter made of a quarter waveplate (QWP2), which has its fast axis
oriented at 90° with respect to QWP1 and a linear polarizer (LP2) in cross-polarization with respect
to LP1. This polarization filter is used to eliminate non-converted light passing through the
metasurface. In the reference arm, the beam passes through a (HWP) that rotates the polarization
of the laser beam from horizontal to vertical and it then is sent to a 5x beam expander (BE). The
reference beam and the OAM beam are then recombined via a second 50:50 beam-splitter (BS2)
and imaged on the camera. The interference of the two beams results in the measured characteristic
spiral interference pattern (as seen in Fig. 3 and Fig. 5). In order to ensure the time overlap between
the two beams, the optical path in one arm of the interferometer was adjusted using a delay line.

In Supplementary Fig. 1(b), the optical setup used to examine the photonic spin Hall effect is
demonstrated. Same femto-second laser is adopted as light source. A ND filter is also used to
attenuate the background. A horizontally-polarized beam is subsequently produced by a linear
polarizer (LP1) and it passes through a quarter waveplate (QWP1) to produce a circularly polarized
beam. After passes through a 20× objective lens, light is effectively focused on the metasurface,
and the transmitted beam is collected by another 20× objective lens. Then, the beam passes through
a quarter waveplate (QWP2), which has its fast axis oriented at 90° with respect to QWP1, and a
linear polarizer (LP2) to eliminate the undesired polarization. Eventually, spin dependent splitting
is captured by the camera after passing through a focusing lens (L1, f=150 mm). It is worth
mentioning that the generally low polarization conversion efficiency of our sample results in a
relatively strong co-polarized transmission component, which remains detectable after passing
through the linear polarizer, and form the 0th order diffraction captured in photonic spin-Hall effect.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In this work, the authors demonstrate that PB phase in metasurfaces can be topologically reconstructed by encircling EPs in the complex plane of certain cross-polarization channel in the circular polarization basis. Three SOI mechanisms are numerically and experimentally verified, including chiral SOI of suppression, inversion, and doubling, manifesting by metasurface functionalities of wavelength- and polarization-dependent OAM control and beam steering. The idea is very interesting, which reveals a new perspective in understanding and designing the chiral phase responses for broader applications. However, the presentation requires further improvement in clarity, precision, and structural organization. Before the final decision, the following comments should be addressed.
1. The PB phase acquisition is strongly affected by the EP. However, the cross-polarization amplitude is also affected, as EP corresponds to the zero cross-polarization conversion point. This would bring influence to the desired functionalities. The authors should clarify and provide discussion on this point.
2. Only the amplitude and phase distributions of one cross-polarization channel in the wavelength-angle space are presented in each steering mechanism. It is necessary to present the corresponding results in the other cross-polarization channel for clear comparison.
3. One of the core ideas and key contributions of this work is the complex plane perspective for reinterpreting the PB phase accumulation. However, the authors place this discussion in the Supplementary Materials, which significantly weakens the readability and impact of the manuscript. I strongly recommend presenting this key concept and content in the main text, with concise formulas and clear descriptions, while leaving the detailed derivations in the Supplementary Materials.
4. It will be helpful if the authors provide the resonance analysis at the EP points and offer a clear explanation of the physical origin of the EP phenomena.
5. Can the authors talk about the underline mechanism of why the emergence of such an EP can steer the PB phase response? Besides, it seems that the SOI suppression likely emerges between the wavelength range of two EPs, and the two EPs have opposite “handedness” in the wavelength-angle space. Could the authors also check this point, since it determines whether the SOI suppression effect is induced by single or dual EPs?
6. Are the laser spots in the middle parts of Fig. 5c caused by the 0t-order diffraction of the co-polarized transmission? If yes, why its influence on the vortex beam generations is hard to observe?
7. In Fig. 3Eiii and 3Fiii, the experimental results for chiral SOI doubling seems not clear without the aid of the white dashed guidelines. It may be more straightforward to be demonstrated using photonic spin-Hall effect, where the deflection angle will be enlarged under LCP incidence.
8. In the conclusion, the authors state their method can be used in information-encryption. However, related information in the main text and Supplementary Materials is quite not enough, which reads confusing and weakens the narrative. It is meaningful if the authors give an metasurface design example to show the encrypt ability, either in simulation or experiment.
9. It will be helpful if the authors present the corresponding meta-atom schematics in Fig. 2 and Fig. 4, and give out their dimensions in the main text. This can make a clearer guidance to the readers. It is quite easy to be confused that Fig. 2Ai and Fig. 2Bi are the two cross-polarized transmission results of the same rotation meta-atom.
10. Some other small suggestions:
a) The definitions of the signs of “+ and –”, the abbreviations of CCW and CW, should be defined in the main text.
b) The authors state that “PB phase are widely used in metasurfaces…to exhibit SOI phenomena, such as the spin Hall effect…” However, the term of “spin Hall effect” should be used more precisely as “photonic spin Hall effect”.
c) The thickness of the ITO film mentioned in the main text (160 nm) and the methods (150 nm) are different. The material parameters of the metal structures and the ITO film should also be presented.
d) The tick marks of the axes in Fig. 2A(i,ii), Fig. 2B(i,ii), and Fig. 4A,4B are not clear, and the label of the horizontal axes are also not presented. Besides, the axes of all the simulated and measured results, as well as corresponding scalebars should be presented.
e) In Fig. 2Ai and 2Bi, the mapping of t−+ and t+− are not presented in an intuitive manner. I suggest that the authors provide, in the Supplementary Materials, all line plots versus wavelength at the angles where the EP points occur.
f) In Fig. 3 and Fig. 5, the authors present the interference pattern to characterize the vortex beam features. It will be good if authors also include the corresponding intensity distributions without interference from the reference beam.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The author innovatively proposed a design scheme for achieving nonlinear PB phase by introducing perturbations to construct EP points in chiral metasurfaces, and elaborated on the underlying principles. The selection of the relative position between the EP point and the incident wavelength was demonstrated to suppress, reverse, and double the SOI effect, and experimental verification was carried out. The theoretical foundation is robust and the approach demonstrates significant innovation. However, the following questions require solution prior to publication:
1. Page 7, line 143: Please explain why SOI suppression in Figure 2A occurs between 700 and 750 nm. However, SOI suppression occurs from 790 to 710 nm under RCP incidence. Does SOI suppression occur at wavelengths below 700 nm? Could you provide the wavelength ranges for which SOI suppression does and does not occur?
2. Could you add |t-+| and arg[t-+] for metasurface 2A, and |t+-| and arg[t+-] for metasurface 2B in the supplementary material.
3. For metasurface 2A, the phase distribution in Figure 2Aii shows that the phase variation with rotation angle within a 2π range at an incident wavelength of 790 nm has little correlation with the EP point at 750 nm, and the region surrounding the EP point does not appear to be the EP point at 750 nm. Is it possible to obtain a 2π phase modulation range at approximately 740 nm?
4. According to Figure 2Bi, the EP generation point does not seem to be at 819.55 nm, but at least exceeds 825 nm. Please correct the wavelength of the EP point or the drawing method.
5. The two light spots shown in Figures 3C and 3D are rather odd. Is one of them the center point?
6. Figure 2(C-D)iv shows the generation of multiple EP points and should not be placed in this section, and this section does not discuss this figure.
7. Why are Au and TIO materials chosen for the metasurface in the paper? Can the emergence of EP and the introduction of interference be achieved with all-dielectric materials such as Si or Ge?
8. For the metasurface in Figure 2B, at an incident wavelength of 689.22 nm, two circles around the EP point exhibit a phase variation of 4π. However, in Figure 3Eiii, the wavelength at which the doubled PB phase appears is 730 nm. The meta-atom corresponding to the every results in Figures 3 should be clarified in the figure legend.
9. Is the doubled PB phase in Figure 3E induced by the presence of two EPs in Figure 2B? If so, would this structure be better addressed in the "Dual EPs induced topological reconstruction" section? On the other hand, are the opposite PB phases due to the presence of two EPs at different frequencies? If so, could you please explain in the manuscript the specific EPs induce the PB phase doubling in each of these three phenomena?
10. Why can elliptical metal columns introduce interference behavior, and why can the elliptical particles maintain their original nonlinear characteristics when the main structure rotates while the main structure does not rotate? Please briefly explain this principle in the paper.
11. The adopted meta-atoms in the manuscript involves many parameters. How to determine the structural size parameters during the design process? Are there any theoretical reference values?
12. The descriptions of the horizontal and vertical axes in Figure 2 are missing. The vertical axis in Figure 2D ranges from -3 to 3. Are the units in radians? The horizontal axis is in degrees. It is recommended that the units used be clearly indicated in the descriptions of the horizontal and vertical axes.
13. Figure S7 and legend are separated in the supporting materials.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Dear reviewers:
Thank you for taking the time to review our manuscript entitled “Chiral
Spin-Orbit-Interactions Steering via EP induced topological reconstruction”
(Manuscript ID: NCOMMS- 25-67039-T).
We greatly appreciate your valuable comments and suggestions, which have been
carefully considered in our revisions. Below, we have provided a point-by-point
response, along with the corresponding changes made in the revised manuscript and
supplementary materials for your reference. We believe that all the comments have
been addressed, the revised manuscript meets the standard of Nature Communicaitons
for publication.
Reply to Reviewer 1:
General Comment: In this work, the authors demonstrate that PB phase in
metasurfaces can be topologically reconstructed by encircling EPs in the complex
plane of certain cross-polarization channel in the circular polarization basis.
Three SOI mechanisms are numerically and experimentally verified, including
chiral SOI of suppression, inversion, and doubling, manifesting by metasurface
functionalities of wavelength- and polarization-dependent OAM control and
beam steering. The idea is very interesting, which reveals a new perspective in
understanding and designing the chiral phase responses for broader applications.
However, the presentation requires further improvement in clarity, precision,
and structural organization. Before the final decision, the following comments
should be addressed.
Responses:
We greatly appreciate your positive comments and detailed summary of our work.
Many of the suggestions you have given us are enlightening our research. We have
carefully revised and proofread the manuscript according to your suggestions.
Below is a more detailed reply and revisions. The revised sentences are
highlighted in red and added to the revised manuscript, while the sentences in
black remain unchanged. Deleted sentences are marked in black with a
strikethrough.
Comments1: The PB phase acquisition is strongly affected by the EP. However,
the cross-polarization amplitude is also affected, as EP corresponds to the zero
cross-polarization conversion point. This would bring influence to the desired
functionalities. The authors should clarify and provide discussion on this point.
Responses:
We greatly appreciate your comments. The cross-polarization amplitude is
affected by the EP, as the EP corresponds to the zero cross-polarization conversion
point. We assume you are worried that this might influence the phenomena discussed
in our manuscript. Below, we will provide a detailed response to address this issue,
and we have made corresponding modifications to both the main text and
supplementary materials to include a more thorough discussion of this point.
In response to this concern, we would like to clarify that while it is true that
passing through the EP involves encountering states with low cross-polarization
amplitude, this does not affect the desired functionalities according to our theoretical
analysis. Specifically, the winding number of the PB phase acquisition process is only
influenced by the zero cross-polarization conversion point (the EP), not by the low
cross-polarization conversion rate (PCR) at intermediate states. Therefore, the low
PCR observed during the rotation process cannot steer the PB phase-mediated
spin-orbit interaction (SOI) processes. It merely indicates low cross-polarization
conversion efficiency at the corresponding rotation angle.
This conclusion can be verified by examining the encircling trajectory in the
cross-polarization conversion complex plane, along with the PB phase response and
PCR at the relevant wavelength. Fig. R1(A, B) details the PCR and PB phase across
the wavelength-angle space, with three specific wavelengths examined: 756.89 nm
(red line), 749.37 nm (yellow line), and 738.10 nm (blue line), as shown in Fig.
R1(C-E). In Fig. R1(C), the cross-polarization amplitude in panel (i) is low but does
not reach the EP (marked by the blue circle). The corresponding trajectory in the
complex plane (panel (ii)) encircles the EP, yielding a winding number of -1.
Consequently, the resulting PB phase accumulation (panel (iii)) follows a
conventional profile. Fig. R1(D) shows the case where the EP is reached. Here, the
encircling trajectory (panel (ii)) passes directly through the EP. This condition
prevents the PB phase from achieving a full 2π modulation range, as shown in panel
(iii). Despite the similarly low cross-polarization amplitude in panel (i) of Fig. R1(E)
and (C), their trajectories in panel (ii) differ fundamentally. The trajectory in Fig.
R1(E) does not enclose the EP, yielding a winding number of 0. Therefore, as panel
(iii) demonstrates, the PB phase accumulation is suppressed.
Fig. R1. The influence of low PCR on TR-PB phase. (A and B) The PCR and PB
phase response at wavelength-angle space. We fixed the wavelength at the positions
of the red (756.89 nm), yellow (749.37) and blue (738.10 nm) dotted lines to
investigate the influence of PCR on the desired functionalities. (C-E) The
cross-polarization conversion rate, encircling trajectory in the cross-polarization
conversion complex plane and corresponding PB phase response at different
wavelength.
In summary, the standard PB phase acquisition is preserved as long as the
winding number is preserved, even when the PCR is low. Only after passing through
the EP can the winding number be altered, leading to the desired steering
functionalities. The low PCR after passing through the EP is a collateral effect of
inducing the EP and does not cause any changes in the winding number. As a result,
low PCR has no impact on the topologically reconstructed PB (TR-PB) phase
response or the desired functionalities. This behavior is consistent across the entire
study.
Changes in the manuscript:
We add one sentence in the main text before Fig.3 to provide the corresponding
discussion.
“Since the winding number only changes upon traversing an EP, the corresponding
low PCR around such transition has no impact on the TR-PB phase response. See
supplementary note 6 for a complete discussion.”
We also add supplementary note in the supplementary materials with the subtitle
“6. The influence of low PCR on TR-PB phase.” to provide a more detailed
discussion.

cross-polarization conversion rate (PCR) does not steer the PB phase-mediated SOI

(blue line), as shown in Fig. S11(C-E).
In Fig. S11(C), the cross-polarization amplitude in panel (i) is low but does not reach
the EP (marked by the blue circle). The corresponding trajectory in the complex plane

Responses:
We appreciate your constructive comment. The physical origin of the EP
phenomena has been explained in previous studies (Science 373.6559: 1133-1137
(2021), Nat. Commun. 15.1: 232 (2024)), which states that the EP arises when
opposite and equal surface current distribution occur along one direction, while the
surface current of the other orthogonal direction exists. By changing the geometric
parameters or input wavelength, such near field behavior results in a zero
cross-polarization conversion. However, the structure that we employ have never been
scrutinized. Here, we offer a near field analysis of our structure by examining the
surface current distribution.
Fig. R3. Near-field analysis of the EP origin. (A) Schematic of the meta-atom with
a 51º rotated main structure. The red and black lines mark the cross sections analyzed
at the top and bottom layers, respectively. (B) Cross-polarization conversion rate
versus input wavelength. The five analyzed wavelengths are marked by solid circles,
with the EP state highlighted in light-red. (C, D) Surface current distributions on the
corresponding cross sections at each wavelength. The insets show the effective
current (black arrows). (E) Evolution of the net surface current, where the EP
emergence is indicated by the light-red highlight.
By examining the surface currents on the top and bottom layers (marked in red
and black in Fig. R3(A), respectively), we elucidate the physical origin of the
exceptional points (EPs) through the mechanism consistent with prior studies. As
shown in Fig. R3(B), an EP can be accessed by tuning the wavelength. We analyze
the five representative wavelengths marked in solid circles, with the corresponding
surface current behaviors displayed in Fig. R3(C–D), i-v.
As the wavelength increases continuously, the top layer current along the
lower-left direction weakens and eventually reverses, while its orthogonal component
remains nearly constant. The effective surface current for this process is indicated by
black arrows in the insets of Fig. R3(C, i–v). In contrast, the bottom-layer current
evolves differently: with increasing wavelength, the surface current component along
the upper-right direction strengthens while the orthogonal component diminishes. The
resulting effective current is similarly denoted by black arrows in Fig. R3(D, i–v).
The net surface current is summarized in Fig. R3(E). As the wavelength rises, one
directional component of the net current gradually vanishes, leaving only the
orthogonal component. Such state signals the emergence of an EP and is highlighted
in light red in Fig. R3(B, E-iii). With further increase in wavelength, the net current
grows along the opposite (upper-right) direction, and the EP vanishes.

By examining the surface currents on the top and bottom layers (marked in red and

points (EPs) through the mechanism consistent with prior studies. As shown in Fig.
S16(B), an EP can be accessed by tuning the wavelength. We analyze the five

current behaviors displayed in Fig. S16(C–D), i-v.
As the wavelength increases continuously, the top layer current along the lower-left

Comments5: Can the authors talk about the underline mechanism of why the
emergence of such an EP can steer the PB phase response? Besides, it seems that
the SOI suppression likely emerges between the wavelength range of two EPs,
and the two EPs have opposite “handedness” in the wavelength-angle space.
Could the authors also check this point, since it determines whether the SOI
suppression effect is induced by single or dual EPs?
Responses:
Thank you very much for your comment. To provide a clearer and more
organized response to your comment, we have broken it down into two parts and will
address each point separately.
(1) “Can the authors talk about the underline mechanism of why the emergence of
such an EP can steer the PB phase response?”
The underlying mechanism behind the change in the winding number is closely
related to the emergence of the EP. In the absence of a zero cross-polarization
conversion point, the PB phase accumulation process remains topologically protected,
meaning the PB phase response stays conventional and cannot be steered or altered.
Fig. R4. The schematics for demonstrating the underline mechanism of TR-PB
phase steering. (A) The PB-mediated SOI process is topologically protected. No
matter how the rotation angle and wavelength vary, the winding number remain fixed.
(B) After inducing EP during rotation, the topological protection is disrupted, and the
PB phase acquisition cannot cover the scope of 2π. (C) The winding number is
changed to 0 by EP induction, and hence leading to SOI suppression.
For example, Fig. R4(A) shows that a single EP emerges at a specific wavelength
during rotation of the main structure. As illustrated in Fig. R4(B), traversing this EP
changes the winding number from 1 to 0. As a result, the shaded areas cannot be
reached by the encirclement as shown in Fig. R4 (B, C). Thus the maximum phase
manipulation caused by rotation is limited to a rather small range, which renders the
PB phase largely insusceptible to rotation. Consequently, it leads to the suppression of
the spin-orbit interaction, as shown in Fig. R4(C). Further discussion is provided in
supplementary note 1.3.
(2) “it seems that the SOI suppression likely emerges between the wavelength range
of two EPs, and the two EPs have opposite “handedness” in the wavelength-angle
space. Could the authors also check this point, since it determines whether the SOI
suppression effect is induced by single or dual EPs?”
The two EPs that emerge at different wavelengths share the same handedness,
with one serving to “close” and the other to “re-open” the TR-PB phase response.
Alternatively, they participate in the SOI suppression process through opposite
topological manipulation. To enhance clarity, we differentiate the chirality of the EPs
using distinct line types: the solid circle represents the REP (right-handed EP),
while the dashed circle denotes the LEP (left-handed EP).
Fig. R5. EPs in the wavelength-angle space. (A, D) PCR and PB phase response
during the SOI suppression process. (B, E) PCR and PB phase response during the
SOI suppression and doubling processes. (C, F) PCR and PB phase response during
the SOI inversion process. Solid circles denote REPs, while the dashed circles
indicate LEPs. Red EPs increase the winding number, whereas black EPs decrease it
as the wavelength decreases.
The opposite “handedness” of the EPs in the wavelength-angle space reflects
changes in the winding number. For instance, in Fig. R5(E), the winding number is +1
above 819.55 nm. During the transition from longer to shorter wavelengths, after
passing the first EP at 819.55 nm, which shows a clockwise phase increment, the
winding number drops to 0, corresponding to SOI suppression. This value persists
until the introduction of the second EP at 704.26 nm, where a counterclockwise phase
increment restores the winding number to +1, effectively “re-opening” the SOI
process. Subsequently, after traversing the third EP at 691.73 nm, which also exhibits
a counterclockwise phase increment, the winding number increases to +2, leading to
SOI doubling. Finally, passing through the fourth EP at 681.7 nm, characterized by a
clockwise phase increment, returns the winding number to +1, thereby terminating the
doubling effect. Thus, a counterclockwise phase increment at an EP increases the
winding number, while a clockwise increment decreases it.
It is worth emphasizing that although EPs may exhibit opposite phase-increment
directions and perform opposing topological manipulations, they share the same
handedness, as each occurs at a point where t
− +
= 0 or t
+ −
= 0 . To facilitate the
identification of EPs, they are color-coded based on their role in the topological
reconstruction of PB phase: as wavelength decreases, red indicates EPs that
increase the winding number by +1, while black represents those that decrease it
by -1.

Comments6: Are the laser spots in the middle parts of Fig. 5c caused by the
0t-order diffraction of the co-polarized transmission? If yes, why its influence on
the vortex beam generations is hard to observe?
Responses:
Thank you very much for your comment. The middle parts in Fig. 5c are caused
by the 0th order diffraction of the co-polarized transmitted light. The primary reason
for this is the generally low polarization conversion efficiency, which results in a
relatively strong co-polarized transmission component that remains detectable after
passing through the linear polarizer.
It is important to recognize that this portion of the 0th-order diffraction does not
engage in the spin-orbit interaction and therefore does not acquire the
Pancharatnam-Berry (PB) phase—a phenomenon well-documented in prior studies
(e.g., Adv. Mater. 37, 2417183 (2025); Nanophotonics 9, 4327–4335 (2020)).
Consequently, when utilizing the PB phase for vortex beam generation, the 0th-order
component associated with the photonic spin Hall effect does not contribute to the
helical phase front of the target vortex beam. Rather, it forms an orthogonally
polarized background. The influence of this orthogonally polarized background is
undetectable in our interference fringe patterns, since the reference beam shares the
polarization of the vortex beam, preventing significant contrast modulation by the
background.

through the linear polarizer and contributes to the 0th-order diffraction observed in
the photonic spin-Hall effect.”

Comments8: In the conclusion, the authors state their method can be used in
information-encryption. However, related information in the main text and
Supplementary Materials is quite not enough, which reads confusing and
weakens the narrative. It is meaningful if the authors give an metasurface design
example to show the encrypt ability, either in simulation or experiment.
Responses:
We sincerely thank you for this insightful suggestion. In response, we have
included a design example of information encryption based on TR-PB phase
modulation in Fig. R7. Six distinct meta-atoms are designed, each providing one of
five different PB phase responses, as color-coded in Fig. R7(A). Their PB phase
responses are catalogued by incident polarization and wavelength in a TR-PB phase
library, shown in Fig. R7(B). From such library the PB phase acquisition rule of any
structure under specific polarization and input wavelength can be directly extracted.
Fig. R7(C) illustrates the encryption design workflow. A modified GS algorithm
first computes the near-field phase distributions of the decoy image and the hidden
image. The two phase-profiles are linked through the rules of reversed, doubled, and
conventional PB phase accumulation. By comparing the two distributions, a ternary
mask consisting only of values “-1”, “+1”, and “+2” is obtained. By consulting the
TR-PB library, every specific meta-atom type of the metasurface and the rotation
angle of each main structure are determined, together with the correct decryption key
K (σ, λ) that encodes the required polarization and wavelength. As shown in
at 730 nm, where both phase inversion and doubling occur, RCP illumination switches
the reconstructed hologram from “cat” to “dog,” whereas illumination with opposite
handedness merely yields an inverted “cat” (Fig. R7(D)i-ii).

meta-atoms. (B) Library of TR-PB phase responses, sorted by polarization and input
wavelength. (C) Design example of the encryption scheme. Using a modified GS
algorithm, the near-field phase distributions for the decoy image and the hidden image
are generated. By comparing the two phase distributions and referencing the TR-PB
phase library, the final arrangement adopting the six available meta-atoms (including
the rotation angle of each main structure) is obtained. (D) Decryption demonstration.
Wrong key leads to decoy results, and only by using the correct key, can the hidden
message be retrieved, as shown in the red dotted box in Fig.R7(D), ⅳ.

Comments1: Page 7, line 143: Please explain why SOI suppression in Figure 2A
occurs between 700 and 750 nm. However, SOI suppression occurs from 790 to
710 nm under RCP incidence. Does SOI suppression occur at wavelengths below
700 nm? Could you provide the wavelength ranges for which SOI suppression
does and does not occur?
Responses:
We greatly appreciate your comment. The SOI suppression occurs specifically
within the 700-750 nm wavelength range due to the presence of two exceptional
points (EPs) located near 700 nm and 750 nm, respectively. As the wavelength
decreases from 850 nm, the first EP at 750 nm reduces the winding number to zero,
triggering the SOI suppression. The winding number remains unchanged until the
wavelength reaches the second EP near 700 nm, which resets it to -1, thereby
terminating the suppression.
In Fig. 2(A, iv-vii), we employ the photonic spin-Hall effect in simulation to
illustrate this suppression. Representative wavelengths are selected to highlight the
effect. At 790 nm, which is outside the 700-750 nm wavelength range, both RCP and
LCP incident beams are deflected. In contrast, at 710 nm, which is within the 700-750
nm wavelength range, the beam deflection disappears under RCP incidence. For
wavelengths below 700 nm, the suppression is switched off by the second EP, and the
deflection behavior resumes.
A similar mechanism governs the response in Fig. 2(B), except that the distinct
geometry and chirality of the structure shift the effective wavelength band to 706-823
nm, and change the target polarization to LCP. Here, we choose 850 nm and 800 nm
as representative wavelengths to demonstrate the SOI suppression via spin to vortex
conversion. The orbital angular momentum (OAM) generation is clearly observed
outside the 706-823 nm wavelength range, and the OAM generation is suppressed
within the 706-823 nm wavelength range under LCP incidence.
To help readers distinguish between the two designs, we have also added
schematics of the corresponding meta-atoms in Fig. 2(A) and (B), respectively. We
have also added explicit descriptions of the suppression and non-suppression
wavelength ranges in the main text for clarity.

Comments3: For metasurface 2A, the phase distribution in Figure 2Aii shows
that the phase variation with rotation angle within a 2π range at an incident
wavelength of 790 nm has little correlation with the EP point at 750 nm, and the
region surrounding the EP point does not appear to be the EP point at 750 nm. Is
it possible to obtain a 2π phase modulation range at approximately 740 nm?
Responses:
We greatly appreciate your comment. At 790 nm, the PB phase still follows the
conventional accumulation and can achieve a full 2π phase modulation range. This is
because the SOI suppression occurs only within the 700-750 nm band, and at 790 nm
the system remains unaffected by the exceptional point (EP) at 750 nm, leaving the
PB phase response intact. The simulated result at 790 nm is presented as a
representative wavelength to demonstrate that SOI suppression does not occur outside
the 700-750 nm band; the effect is confined to this interval, as exemplified by our
simulation at 710 nm. Furthermore, the regions adjacent to an EP are not themselves
exceptional points. This is evident from the phase modulation in the wavelength-angle
space shown in Fig. 2A(ii), where only a single EP appears at 749.37 nm.
To further demonstrate such process, we examined the encircling trajectory in the
cross-polarization conversion complex plane, along with the PB phase response and
PCR at the relevant wavelength in Fig. R2. Fig. R2(A, B) details the PCR and PB
phase across the wavelength-angle space, with three specific wavelengths examined:
756.89 nm (red line), 749.37 nm (yellow line), and 738.10 nm (blue line), as shown in
Fig. R2(C-E). In Fig. R2(C), the cross-polarization amplitude in panel (i) is low but does
not reach the EP (marked by the blue circle). The corresponding trajectory in the
complex plane (panel (ii)) encircles the EP, yielding a winding number of -1.
Consequently, the resulting PB phase accumulation (panel (iii)) follows a
conventional profile. Fig. R2(D) shows the case where the EP is reached. Here, the
encircling trajectory (panel (ii)) passes directly through the EP. This condition
prevents the PB phase from achieving a full 2π modulation range, as shown in panel
(iii). Despite the similarly low cross-polarization amplitude in panel (i) of Fig. R2(E)
and (C), their trajectories in panel (ii) differ fundamentally. The trajectory in Fig.
R2(E) does not enclose the EP, yielding a winding number of 0. Therefore, as panel
(iii) demonstrates, the PB phase accumulation is suppressed.
When the incident wavelength is approximately 740 nm, the 2π phase modulation
cannot be obtained, despite there is a phase jump from π to -π observed at
approximately 740 nm in Fig. 2(A),iii. It is because when the encircling trajectory
passes through the EP at 750 nm, the winding number of the encircling trajectory is
diminished to zero. The evolution trajectory in the complex plane perspective offers a
clear insight into such phenomenon. It can be clearly seen in Fig. R2(E),iii, the
trajectory cannot reach all the four quadrants, thus the PB phase accumulation range is
less than π, and the winding number is zero. However, after experiencing EP at 749.37
nm, the winding number is restored to +1, causing regular PB phase response, despite
low cross-polarization rate, as shown in Fig. R2(C),iii.

Responses:
Thank you very much for your comment. The two optical spots correspond to the
0th-order diffraction and the beam deflected by the PB geometric phase, respectively.
Following the design of our metasurface based on the conventional PB phase
accumulation rule, LCP light is deflected to the left, while RCP light is deflected to
the right. Unlike the case of SOI inversion in Fig. 5, which requires displaying both
deflection directions under specific polarizations, here we intentionally omitted the
opposite deflection channels (LCP deflected to the right and RCP deflected to the left)
for clarity. To help the readers identify the center point, we have now marked the
complementary deflection channels to clearly indicate the central position of the effect,
as shown in the revised Fig. 3 below.
The revised Fig. 3 in the main text. The red dashed box highlights the improved photonic
spin-Hall effect results.
The center points in Fig. 3C,D are caused by the 0th order diffraction of the
co-polarized transmitted light. The primary reason for this is the generally low
polarization conversion efficiency, which results in a relatively strong co-polarized
transmission component that remains detectable after passing through the linear
polarizer.
It is important to recognize that this portion of the 0th-order diffraction does not
engage in the spin-orbit interaction and therefore does not acquire the
Pancharatnam-Berry (PB) phase. Such phenomenon is well-documented in prior
studies (e.g., Adv. Mater. 37, 2417183 (2025); Nanophotonics 9, 4327–4335 (2020)).
Consequently, when utilizing the PB phase for vortex beam generation, the 0th-order
component associated with the photonic spin Hall effect does not contribute to the
helical phase front of the target vortex beam. Rather, it forms an orthogonally
polarized background. The influence of this orthogonally polarized background is
undetectable in our interference fringe patterns, since the reference beam shares the
polarization of the vortex beam, preventing significant contrast modulation by the
background.

Fig. 1. Novel chiral SOI phenomena. ……”
Comments7: Why are Au and ITO materials chosen for the metasurface in the
paper? Can the emergence of EP and the introduction of interference be
achieved with all-dielectric materials such as Si or Ge?
Responses:
Thank you for raising the point regarding material selection. The emergence of
exceptional points (EPs) is fundamentally a phenomenon arising from the degeneracy
of eigenvalues and eigenstates in the Jones matrix, and is not exclusive to metallic
structures. Indeed, all-dielectric materials such as silicon (Si) or germanium (Ge) can
also support EPs, as has been demonstrated in recent literature (Light: Science &
Applications 14, 262 (2025)).
In our work, the operational wavelength was designed for the visible to
near-infrared range (corresponding to our laser source Ti: Sapphire ultrafast
femtosecond laser centered at 800 nm). The Au-ITO configuration was therefore
selected to ensure optimal resonance matching and experimental feasibility within our
target spectral regime. We fully agree that all-dielectric platforms offer a promising
alternative, particularly at longer wavelengths or in low-loss applications, and
appreciate the reviewer's suggestion for potential extensions of this work.
Changes in the manuscript:
We changed the 47th reference to demonstrate such EP is not exclusive to
metallic structures：

Phase Through Low-Voltage Operation on Conductive Polymer. Adv. Funct. Mater. ,
2501916 (2025).
47. Yi, C., Wang, Z., Shi, Y. et al. Creating topological exceptional point by on-chip
all-dielectric metasurface. Light-Sci Appl 14, 262 (2025).”
Comments8: For the metasurface in Figure 2B, at an incident wavelength of
689.22 nm, two circles around the EP point exhibit a phase variation of 4π.
However, in Figure 3Eiii, the wavelength at which the doubled PB phase appears
is 730 nm. The meta-atom corresponding to the every results in Figures 3 should
be clarified in the figure legend.
Responses:
Thank you very much for your comment. The spectral shift in the doubling
phenomenon is explained in the last section of our original manuscript. The spectral
shift of chiral SOI doubling phenomenon from 690 nm (simulated in Fig. 2D, iv) to
730 nm in experiment arises from the interplay of two factors. First, disrupting the
topological protection of PB phase accumulation with one EP (leading to a winding
number of 0) destabilizes EP encircling evolution in an uncontrollable manner on the
polarization- conversion complex plane. It means the actual evolution trajectory in
experiment is not the same as the simulation. Second, fabrication errors and
inhomogeneities of meta- atoms also amplify such deviations from simulated
trajectories in Fig. 2C, iv.
In addition, the meta-atoms corresponding to the results in Fig. 3 are illustrated
in Fig. 3A-B. Specifically, the results shown in Fig. 3C–D were obtained from a
metasurface composed of the meta-atom depicted in Fig. 3A, while those in Fig. 3E–F
originate from the structure shown in Fig. 3B. Although the meta-atoms shown in the
SEM pictures differ in orientation, they share identical geometric parameters.
Changes in the manuscript:
We have revised the figure legend of Figure 3.
“Fig. 3. The experimental results of chiral SOI suppression and doubling. (A and B)
Scanning electron micrographs (SEMs) of fabricated metasurface for demonstrating
chiral SOI suppression and doubling. (C and D) Corresponding to Fig. 3A, i to ⅱ are
the measured diffraction patterns of spin-Hall effect, under the excitation of LCP and
RCP light with wavelengths of 790 nm and 710 nm. (E and F) Corresponding to Fig.
3B, i to ⅲ are the interference patterns under excitation of LCP and RCP light with
wavelengths of 850 nm, 800 nm, and 730 nm. The red (blue) shaded area represents
LCP (RCP) incidence.”
Comments9: Is the doubled PB phase in Figure 3E induced by the presence of
two EPs in Figure 2B? If so, would this structure be better addressed in the
"Dual EPs induced topological reconstruction" section? On the other hand, are
the opposite PB phases due to the presence of two EPs at different frequencies?
If so, could you please explain in the manuscript the specific EPs induce the PB
phase doubling in each of these three phenomena?
Responses:
Thank you for this insightful comment. The doubled PB phase observed in Fig.
3E is not induced by the presence of two EPs at different frequencies, but rather
induced by a single EP with counterclockwise phase increment at 691 nm (in red
dashed circle) in the wavelength angle space, and is restored to normal by a single EP
with clockwise phase increment at 681 nm (in black dashed circle). Using winding
number analysis, we can clearly see that one EP activates the SOI doubling and the
other deactivates it. It is analogous to how SOI suppression is turned on and off by the
two EPs at different wavelengths.
Similarly, the reversed PB phase are caused by the dual EPs under a fixed
wavelength, and not by the two EPs at different wavelength. At 748.12 nm, both of
the two EPs increase the winding number, thus the winding number is changed from
-1 to +1. At 691.73 nm, both of the two EPs decrease the winding number, thus the
winding number is changed from +1 back to -1.
To help the readers better distinguish the EPs, each EP is assigned a specific
color according to their role in the topological reconstruction of PB phase: red for
those increasing the winding number by +1, and black for those decreasing it by
-1, as wavelength decreases. In addition, the chirality of the EPs is distinguished
using different linetypes: The solid circle represents the REP (right-handed EP),
while the dashed circle denotes the LEP (left-handed EP).
Fig. R5. EPs in the wavelength-angle space. (A, D) PCR and PB phase response
during the SOI suppression process. (B, E) PCR and PB phase response during the
SOI suppression and doubling processes. (C, F) PCR and PB phase response during
the SOI inversion process. Solid circles denote REPs, while the dashed circles
indicate LEPs. Red EPs increase the winding number, whereas black EPs decrease it
as the wavelength decreases.
For instance, in Fig. R5(E), the winding number is +1 above 819.55 nm. During
the transition from longer to shorter wavelengths, after passing the first EP at 819.55
nm, which shows a clockwise phase increment, the winding number drops to 0,
corresponding to SOI suppression. This value persists until the introduction of the
second EP at 704.26 nm, where a counterclockwise phase increment restores the
winding number to +1, effectively “re-opening” the SOI process. Subsequently, after
traversing the third EP at 691.73 nm, which also exhibits a counterclockwise phase
increment, the winding number increases to +2, leading to SOI doubling. Finally,
passing through the fourth EP at 681.7 nm, characterized by a clockwise phase
increment, returns the winding number to +1, thereby terminating the doubling effect.

We add some sentences to the last paragraph before Fig. 3 to emphasize the
identification of EP types.
“It is worth pointing out that EPs despite sharing the same handedness, they may
exhibit opposite phase-increment in the wavelength-angle space, which reflects the
opposing topological manipulations. For instance, in Fig. 2B, ii-iii, the SOI
suppression is caused by the black dashed EP at 823 nm, and is closed by the red
dashed EP at 705 nm. The SOI doubling is caused by the red dashed EP at 691 nm,
and is closed by the black dashed EP at 681 nm. Since the winding number only
changes upon traversing an EP, the corresponding low PCR around such transition
has no impact on the TR-PB phase response. See supplementary note 6 for a complete
discussion.”
Comments10: Why can elliptical metal columns introduce interference behavior,
and why can the elliptical particles maintain their original nonlinear
characteristics when the main structure rotates while the main structure does not
rotate? Please briefly explain this principle in the paper.
Responses:
Thank you for raising this question regarding the working mechanism of the
perturbation ellipses. The fixed elliptical structure introduces perturbation because its
coupling with the main structure varies with rotation of the main structure. Since EP
itself is sensitive against perturbation, such coupling modulation can effectively tailor
the EP response, enabling the proposed SOI steering processes.
It should be clarified that the elliptical structures in our design function as a
linear perturbation element and do not exhibit nonlinear properties in this context.
They serve primarily as a geometric tool to modulate rotation symmetry and introduce
orientation-dependent coupling, without involving nonlinear optical effects. We will
include a concise explanation of this principle in the revised manuscript to improve
clarity.
Changes in the manuscript:
We add some words and sentences to the last paragraph of introduction in the
main text to emphasize the working mechanism of the perturbation ellipses.
“By introducing static elliptical perturbations, a rotational anisotropy is induced, as
their coupling to the main structure changes with rotation. This ensures that the
encircling trajectory avoids full EP collapse, encountering EPs only at discrete points.
Such encounters disrupt topological protection, change the winding number, and
trigger three novel steering mechanisms:”
Comments11: The adopted meta-atoms in the manuscript involves many
parameters. How to determine the structural size parameters during the design
process? Are there any theoretical reference values?
Responses:
Thank you very much for your insightful comment. The determination of
geometric parameters for the meta-atoms is indeed a key step in achieving the desired
TR-PB phase response and SOI steering functionalities.
In our design workflow, the structural parameters are obtained through a
systematic series of parameter sweeps using finite-difference time-domain (FDTD)
simulations. Specifically, we first fix the distances between the two “L” structures (dx
and dy), and then sweep the arm lengths l1 and l2 to identify the emergence of
cross-polarization conversion singularities across the wavelength range. These
singularities correspond to the formation of EPs. If no EP appears within this initial
parameter space, we then adjust dx and dy and repeat the l1–l2 sweeps. By iteratively
refining this two-stage parameter search, EPs with the desired handedness and
wavelength position can be reliably located and selected as the main strucutre’s
geometric parameters. After determining the main structure, we introduce the
perturbation element and explore its relative displacement and geometric size.
Through sweeping these parameters, we construct the wavelength–angle space maps
(e.g., Fig. 2A(i)) and identify configurations that exhibit clear PB-phase manipulation
and SOI steering characteristics. It is important to emphasize that this workflow is
primarily simulation-driven and does not rely on predetermined theoretical reference
values. Instead, the EP centered design principle serves as the guiding criterion for
parameter selection, enabling efficient identification of structures that support the
desired topological reconstruction of the PB phase.
Moreover, our configuration that realize EP response can be explained by a near
field analysis via examining the surface current distribution.
By examining the surface currents on the top and bottom layers (marked in red
and black in Fig. R6(A), respectively), we elucidate the physical origin of the
exceptional points (EPs) through the mechanism consistent with prior studies. As
shown in Fig. R6(B), an EP can be accessed by tuning the wavelength. We analyze
the five representative wavelengths marked in solid circles, with the corresponding
surface current behaviors displayed in Fig. R6(C–D), i-v.
As the wavelength increases continuously, the top layer current along the
lower-left direction weakens and eventually reverses, while its orthogonal component
remains nearly constant. The effective surface current for this process is indicated by
black arrows in the insets of Fig. R6(C, i–v). In contrast, the bottom-layer current
evolves differently: with increasing wavelength, the surface current component along
the upper-right direction strengthens while the orthogonal component diminishes. The
resulting effective current is similarly denoted by black arrows in Fig. R6(D, i–v).
The net surface current is summarized in Fig. R6(E). As the wavelength rises, one
directional component of the net current gradually vanishes, leaving only the
orthogonal component. Such state signals the emergence of an EP and is highlighted
in light red in Fig. R6(B, E-iii). With further increase in wavelength, the net current
grows along the opposite (upper-right) direction, and the EP vanishes.
Fig. R6. Near-field analysis of the EP origin. (A) Schematic of the meta-atom with
a 51º rotated main structure. The red and black lines mark the cross sections analyzed
at the top and bottom layers, respectively. (B) Cross-polarization conversion rate
versus input wavelength. The five analyzed wavelengths are marked by solid circles,
with the EP state highlighted in light-red. (C, D) Surface current distributions on the
corresponding cross sections at each wavelength. The insets show the effective
current (black arrows). (E) Evolution of the net surface current, where the EP
emergence is indicated by the light-red highlight.
