We greatly appreciate your comment. At 790 nm, the PB phase still follows the
conventional accumulation and can achieve a full 2π phase modulation range. This is
because the SOI suppression occurs only within the 700-750 nm band, and at 790 nm
the system remains unaffected by the exceptional point (EP) at 750 nm, leaving the
PB phase response intact. The simulated result at 790 nm is presented as a
representative wavelength to demonstrate that SOI suppression does not occur outside
the 700-750 nm band; the effect is confined to this interval, as exemplified by our
simulation at 710 nm. Furthermore, the regions adjacent to an EP are not themselves
exceptional points. This is evident from the phase modulation in the wavelength-angle
space shown in Fig. 2A(ii), where only a single EP appears at 749.37 nm.
To further demonstrate such process, we examined the encircling trajectory in the
cross-polarization conversion complex plane, along with the PB phase response and
PCR at the relevant wavelength in Fig. R2. Fig. R2(A, B) details the PCR and PB
phase across the wavelength-angle space, with three specific wavelengths examined:
756.89 nm (red line), 749.37 nm (yellow line), and 738.10 nm (blue line), as shown in
Fig. R2(C-E). In Fig. R2(C), the cross-polarization amplitude in panel (i) is low but does
not reach the EP (marked by the blue circle). The corresponding trajectory in the
complex plane (panel (ii)) encircles the EP, yielding a winding number of -1.
Consequently, the resulting PB phase accumulation (panel (iii)) follows a
conventional profile. Fig. R2(D) shows the case where the EP is reached. Here, the
encircling trajectory (panel (ii)) passes directly through the EP. This condition
prevents the PB phase from achieving a full 2π modulation range, as shown in panel
(iii). Despite the similarly low cross-polarization amplitude in panel (i) of Fig. R2(E)
and (C), their trajectories in panel (ii) differ fundamentally. The trajectory in Fig.
R2(E) does not enclose the EP, yielding a winding number of 0. Therefore, as panel
(iii) demonstrates, the PB phase accumulation is suppressed.
When the incident wavelength is approximately 740 nm, the 2π phase modulation
cannot be obtained, despite there is a phase jump from π to -π observed at
approximately 740 nm in Fig. 2(A),iii. It is because when the encircling trajectory
passes through the EP at 750 nm, the winding number of the encircling trajectory is
diminished to zero. The evolution trajectory in the complex plane perspective offers a
clear insight into such phenomenon. It can be clearly seen in Fig. R2(E),iii, the
trajectory cannot reach all the four quadrants, thus the PB phase accumulation range is
less than π, and the winding number is zero. However, after experiencing EP at 749.37
nm, the winding number is restored to +1, causing regular PB phase response, despite
low cross-polarization rate, as shown in Fig. R2(C),iii.

co-polarized transmitted light. The primary reason for this is the generally low
polarization conversion efficiency, which results in a relatively strong co-polarized
transmission component that remains detectable after passing through the linear
polarizer.
It is important to recognize that this portion of the 0th-order diffraction does not
engage in the spin-orbit interaction and therefore does not acquire the
Pancharatnam-Berry (PB) phase. Such phenomenon is well-documented in prior
studies (e.g., Adv. Mater. 37, 2417183 (2025); Nanophotonics 9, 4327–4335 (2020)).
Consequently, when utilizing the PB phase for vortex beam generation, the 0th-order
component associated with the photonic spin Hall effect does not contribute to the
helical phase front of the target vortex beam. Rather, it forms an orthogonally
polarized background. The influence of this orthogonally polarized background is
undetectable in our interference fringe patterns, since the reference beam shares the
polarization of the vortex beam, preventing significant contrast modulation by the
background.

Responses:
Thank you for raising the point regarding material selection. The emergence of
exceptional points (EPs) is fundamentally a phenomenon arising from the degeneracy
of eigenvalues and eigenstates in the Jones matrix, and is not exclusive to metallic
structures. Indeed, all-dielectric materials such as silicon (Si) or germanium (Ge) can
also support EPs, as has been demonstrated in recent literature (Light: Science &
Applications 14, 262 (2025)).
In our work, the operational wavelength was designed for the visible to
near-infrared range (corresponding to our laser source Ti: Sapphire ultrafast
femtosecond laser centered at 800 nm). The Au-ITO configuration was therefore
selected to ensure optimal resonance matching and experimental feasibility within our
target spectral regime. We fully agree that all-dielectric platforms offer a promising
alternative, particularly at longer wavelengths or in low-loss applications, and
appreciate the reviewer's suggestion for potential extensions of this work.

Comments9: Is the doubled PB phase in Figure 3E induced by the presence of
two EPs in Figure 2B? If so, would this structure be better addressed in the
"Dual EPs induced topological reconstruction" section? On the other hand, are
the opposite PB phases due to the presence of two EPs at different frequencies?
If so, could you please explain in the manuscript the specific EPs induce the PB
phase doubling in each of these three phenomena?
Responses:
Thank you for this insightful comment. The doubled PB phase observed in Fig.
3E is not induced by the presence of two EPs at different frequencies, but rather
induced by a single EP with counterclockwise phase increment at 691 nm (in red
dashed circle) in the wavelength angle space, and is restored to normal by a single EP
with clockwise phase increment at 681 nm (in black dashed circle). Using winding
number analysis, we can clearly see that one EP activates the SOI doubling and the
other deactivates it. It is analogous to how SOI suppression is turned on and off by the
two EPs at different wavelengths.
Similarly, the reversed PB phase are caused by the dual EPs under a fixed
wavelength, and not by the two EPs at different wavelength. At 748.12 nm, both of
the two EPs increase the winding number, thus the winding number is changed from
-1 to +1. At 691.73 nm, both of the two EPs decrease the winding number, thus the
winding number is changed from +1 back to -1.
To help the readers better distinguish the EPs, each EP is assigned a specific
color according to their role in the topological reconstruction of PB phase: red for
those increasing the winding number by +1, and black for those decreasing it by
-1, as wavelength decreases. In addition, the chirality of the EPs is distinguished
using different linetypes: The solid circle represents the REP (right-handed EP),
while the dashed circle denotes the LEP (left-handed EP).
Fig. R5. EPs in the wavelength-angle space. (A, D) PCR and PB phase response
during the SOI suppression process. (B, E) PCR and PB phase response during the
SOI suppression and doubling processes. (C, F) PCR and PB phase response during
the SOI inversion process. Solid circles denote REPs, while the dashed circles
indicate LEPs. Red EPs increase the winding number, whereas black EPs decrease it
as the wavelength decreases.
For instance, in Fig. R5(E), the winding number is +1 above 819.55 nm. During
the transition from longer to shorter wavelengths, after passing the first EP at 819.55
nm, which shows a clockwise phase increment, the winding number drops to 0,
corresponding to SOI suppression. This value persists until the introduction of the
second EP at 704.26 nm, where a counterclockwise phase increment restores the
winding number to +1, effectively “re-opening” the SOI process. Subsequently, after
traversing the third EP at 691.73 nm, which also exhibits a counterclockwise phase
increment, the winding number increases to +2, leading to SOI doubling. Finally,
passing through the fourth EP at 681.7 nm, characterized by a clockwise phase
increment, returns the winding number to +1, thereby terminating the doubling effect.

Comments11: The adopted meta-atoms in the manuscript involves many
parameters. How to determine the structural size parameters during the design
process? Are there any theoretical reference values?
Responses:
Thank you very much for your insightful comment. The determination of
geometric parameters for the meta-atoms is indeed a key step in achieving the desired
TR-PB phase response and SOI steering functionalities.
In our design workflow, the structural parameters are obtained through a
systematic series of parameter sweeps using finite-difference time-domain (FDTD)
simulations. Specifically, we first fix the distances between the two “L” structures (dx
and dy), and then sweep the arm lengths l1 and l2 to identify the emergence of
cross-polarization conversion singularities across the wavelength range. These
singularities correspond to the formation of EPs. If no EP appears within this initial
parameter space, we then adjust dx and dy and repeat the l1–l2 sweeps. By iteratively
refining this two-stage parameter search, EPs with the desired handedness and
wavelength position can be reliably located and selected as the main strucutre’s
geometric parameters. After determining the main structure, we introduce the
perturbation element and explore its relative displacement and geometric size.
Through sweeping these parameters, we construct the wavelength–angle space maps
(e.g., Fig. 2A(i)) and identify configurations that exhibit clear PB-phase manipulation
and SOI steering characteristics. It is important to emphasize that this workflow is
primarily simulation-driven and does not rely on predetermined theoretical reference
values. Instead, the EP centered design principle serves as the guiding criterion for
parameter selection, enabling efficient identification of structures that support the
desired topological reconstruction of the PB phase.
Moreover, our configuration that realize EP response can be explained by a near
field analysis via examining the surface current distribution.
By examining the surface currents on the top and bottom layers (marked in red
and black in Fig. R6(A), respectively), we elucidate the physical origin of the
exceptional points (EPs) through the mechanism consistent with prior studies. As
shown in Fig. R6(B), an EP can be accessed by tuning the wavelength. We analyze
the five representative wavelengths marked in solid circles, with the corresponding
surface current behaviors displayed in Fig. R6(C–D), i-v.
As the wavelength increases continuously, the top layer current along the
lower-left direction weakens and eventually reverses, while its orthogonal component
remains nearly constant. The effective surface current for this process is indicated by
black arrows in the insets of Fig. R6(C, i–v). In contrast, the bottom-layer current
evolves differently: with increasing wavelength, the surface current component along
the upper-right direction strengthens while the orthogonal component diminishes. The
resulting effective current is similarly denoted by black arrows in Fig. R6(D, i–v).
The net surface current is summarized in Fig. R6(E). As the wavelength rises, one
directional component of the net current gradually vanishes, leaving only the
orthogonal component. Such state signals the emergence of an EP and is highlighted
in light red in Fig. R6(B, E-iii). With further increase in wavelength, the net current
grows along the opposite (upper-right) direction, and the EP vanishes.
Fig. R6. Near-field analysis of the EP origin. (A) Schematic of the meta-atom with
a 51º rotated main structure. The red and black lines mark the cross sections analyzed
at the top and bottom layers, respectively. (B) Cross-polarization conversion rate
versus input wavelength. The five analyzed wavelengths are marked by solid circles,
with the EP state highlighted in light-red. (C, D) Surface current distributions on the
corresponding cross sections at each wavelength. The insets show the effective
current (black arrows). (E) Evolution of the net surface current, where the EP
emergence is indicated by the light-red highlight.

Comments2: A brief analysis can be provided in the manuscript on how to
increase the cross-polarization conversion rate under the EP mechanism.
Responses:
Thank you for the reviewer for the insightful suggestion. Indeed, under the EP (exceptional
point) mechanism, the cross-polarization conversion rate (PCR) inevitably exhibits
certain local minimum during the rotation process. However, as the reviewer correctly
points out, the overall modulation depth of the PCR can be systematically enhanced
through several approaches.
First, material optimization plays a crucial role. By selecting materials with lower
optical losses at the target wavelength, the intrinsic polarization conversion efficiency
can be improved. For instance, using low-loss dielectric materials or optimizing the
thickness of metallic layers can further boost the PCR baseline.
Second, structural design refinement offers additional degrees of freedom. The
geometry of the meta-atoms can be tailored to maximize the polarization conversion
at the desired operating wavelength or rotation angle. Finite-difference time-domain
(FDTD) simulations can be employed to optimize the parameters, thereby enhancing
the PCR.
Third, the manner in which the EP is introduced during rotation can be further
engineered. Rather than relying on perturbation ellipses, one may design the
metasurface such that the EP is dynamically accessed only at specific rotation angles,
while elsewhere the structure operates away from the EP to maintain high PCR. This
could be achieved by incorporating multiple resonant modes or by exploiting
dispersion engineering to shift the EP wavelength as a function of rotation.
By combining these strategies it is possible to significantly elevate the overall PCR
response of the proposed scheme. We have added a brief discussion of these aspects in
the revised manuscript to address the reviewer's valuable suggestion.

Comments3: It would be beneficial to elaborate further in the section “TR-PB phase
used for information encryption” how this work achieves the spin-decoupling effect at
the wavelength of 730 nm. Specifically, how is the phase of the corresponding pixel in
Fig.6Div determined?
Responses:
Thank you for your comment. The spin-decoupling effect originates from the chiral
nature of the proposed TR-PB phase. Specifically, under the EP response, taking
right-handed EP as an example, the PB phase accumulation rule can be modified from
the conventional −2θ to either −4θ or +2θ under RCP incidence. In contrast, for LCP
incidence, where no EP is excited, the phase accumulation remains the conventional
+2θ rule.
Based on this chiral disparity, we incorporate the distinct phase accumulation rules
into a modified Gerchberg-Saxton (GS) algorithm. The algorithm simultaneously
generates two target near-field phase distributions, one corresponding to the decoy
image and the other to the hidden image, while enforcing that their relationship
follows the above TR-PB phase constraints under RCP and LCP respectively. Through
iterative optimization, the algorithm converges to a metasurface phase profile that
simultaneously satisfies the imaging requirements for both circular polarizations. The
resulting phase distribution for each pixel in Fig. 6(D) iv is therefore determined by
this optimization process, ensuring that the spin-decoupled response is encoded into
the metasurface design.
